lessons.title: The export chain and its requirements
lessons.html:
The export logistics chain

Agricultural exports, such as citrus, deciduous fruit, table grapes, avocados, macadamias, wine and wool, travel long distances to demanding markets. Logistics management ensures the product arrives on time, at the right quality, with the right documents, at an acceptable cost.

Steps in a typical fresh fruit export

  1. Harvest and delivery to the packhouse
  2. Grading, packing and palletising to market specifications
  3. Pre-cooling to the required pulp temperature
  4. Export inspection and certification
  5. Cold storage and consolidation
  6. Road or rail transport to the port (e.g. Durban, Cape Town, Port Elizabeth/Gqeberha) or airport
  7. Container or conventional reefer vessel loading
  8. Sea or air transport
  9. Import clearance, inspection and delivery to the buyer

Key role players

  • Exporter or export agent: markets the product and coordinates logistics.
  • Freight forwarder: books space, arranges transport and documents.
  • Clearing agent: handles customs procedures.
  • Shipping lines and airlines.
  • Cold stores and terminals.
  • PPECB: statutory export quality inspection and cold chain services for perishables.
  • The national department responsible for agriculture: phytosanitary and veterinary export certification.

Market access requirements

  • Phytosanitary requirements of the importing country: pest-free status, specific treatments such as cold treatment protocols for certain pests and markets, and registered production units and packhouses.
  • Maximum residue limits (MRLs) of the importing country, which may differ from local limits.
  • Quality standards under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 and buyer specifications.
  • Certification such as GLOBALG.A.P. and social compliance audits.
  • Labelling and traceability requirements.

Requirements change, so always confirm current protocols with the exporter and the authorities before the season.

lessons.title: Documents, cold chain and risk management
lessons.html:
Key export documents

DocumentPurpose
Commercial invoiceValue of goods, terms, buyer and seller
Packing listContents of each pallet or container
Phytosanitary certificateOfficial confirmation that plant products meet importing country plant health requirements
Export inspection certificateConfirms quality standards were met
Bill of lading or air waybillContract of carriage and receipt for goods
Customs export declarationRequired by SARS
Certificate of originMay be needed to claim preferential tariffs under trade agreements

Errors or missing documents can delay clearance, cause rejection or cost the farm the shipment.

Incoterms

Incoterms define who pays for and bears the risk of each stage. Common examples: FOB (free on board, where the seller's risk ends when goods are loaded on the vessel), CIF (cost, insurance and freight paid by the seller to the destination port), and DAP (delivered at place). Know which term your contract uses.

Managing the cold chain

  • Pre-cool promptly after harvest to the specified temperature.
  • Record pulp temperatures with calibrated probes.
  • Use temperature recorders in containers.
  • Minimise time at ambient temperature during loading.
  • Set container temperature, ventilation and humidity correctly for the commodity.

Risk management

  • Delays: port congestion, weather, strikes. Build in buffer time and maintain good communication with forwarders.
  • Quality claims: keep inspection records, photographs and temperature data as evidence.
  • Currency risk: exporters may use forward cover with banks.
  • Payment risk: letters of credit or reliable agents; export credit insurance.
  • Market access: a single interception of a regulated pest can affect the whole industry.

Planning and performance

Prepare a season logistics plan with expected volumes per week, shipping schedules, cold store capacity and transport bookings. Track performance indicators: on-time shipments, temperature compliance, rejections, claims and cost per carton.

Key points

  • Export logistics run from packhouse to buyer through many role players.
  • Meet phytosanitary, MRL, quality and certification requirements of the importing country.
  • Complete documents accurately: invoice, packing list, phytosanitary and inspection certificates, bill of lading.
  • Understand Incoterms such as FOB and CIF.
  • Protect the cold chain and manage delay, quality, currency and payment risks.
